**Court:** U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit

**Docket Number:** 25-1559

The Department of Commerce determined that the invoice date, not the contract date, was the appropriate “date of sale,” as Kaptan’s own responses indicated that certain material terms, including size breakdowns and quantities, could be modified until shipment or invoicing. Commerce issued a final antidumping duty rate using the invoice date, and the U.S. Court of International Trade upheld this decision.
The Trade Court found that Commerce’s reliance on the invoice date was supported by substantial evidence, including Kaptan’s questionnaire responses and contract documentation, and declined to address whether Commerce exceeded its regulatory authority, as there was no statutory ambiguity at issue. On appeal to the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, Kaptan argued that Commerce’s regulation was an unlawful presumption and that its application was unsupported by substantial evidence.
Consistent with § 351.401(i), Commerce used Kaptan’s invoice date as the date of sale. Doing so, Commerce found that Kaptan had made sales of rebar to the U.S. at prices below normal value and, consequently, assigned Kaptan a preliminary dumping margin of 29.30%.
First, it argues that Commerce exceeded its statutory authority under the Tariff Act by adopting a regulatory presumption that the date of sale is the invoice date. # KAPTAN DEMIR CELIK ENDUSTRISI VE TICARET A.S. v. US , No. 24-1431 (Fed. Cir. 2025)
Annotate this Case

Justia Opinion Summary

Turkish steel producers, including Kaptan Demir Celik Endustrisi ve Ticaret A.S., were subject to a countervailing duty (CVD) order after the U.S. Department of Commerce determined that the Turkish government subsidized steel rebar exports.
The United States Court of International Trade (CIT) reviewed Commerce’s decision after Kaptan challenged the cross-attribution of Nur’s subsidies. The CIT found that Commerce had not adequately explained whether steel scrap was merely a link in the rebar production chain or addressed prior cases treating steel scrap as a byproduct. The CIT remanded the case for further explanation.
As a result, Commerce concluded that Nur was not a cross-owned input supplier, and Kaptan’s CVD rate was reduced to a de minimis level. The CIT sustained Commerce’s remand decision. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit reviewed the CIT’s decision for abuse of discretion and Commerce’s remand findings for substantial evidence.
The Federal Circuit affirmed, holding that Commerce’s determination that Nur’s steel scrap was not primarily dedicated to Kaptan’s rebar production was adequately explained, supported by substantial evidence, and consistent with the applicable regulation.

US  Turkish steel producers, including Kaptan Demir Celik Endustrisi ve Ticaret A.S., were subject to a countervailing duty (CVD) order after the U.S. Department of Commerce determined that the Turkish government subsidized steel rebar exports. During an administrative review, Commerce found that Kaptan sourced steel scrap, a key input for rebar, from several affiliates, including Nur, a shipbuilder. Commerce initially determined that Nur’s steel scrap was primarily dedicated to Kaptan’s rebar production, making Nur a cross-owned input supplier whose subsidies should be attributed to Kaptan, thereby increasing Kaptan’s CVD rate.The United States Court of International Trade (CIT) reviewed Commerce’s decision after Kaptan challenged the cross-attribution of Nur’s subsidies. The CIT found that Commerce had not adequately explained whether steel scrap was merely a link in the rebar production chain or addressed prior cases treating steel scrap as a byproduct. The CIT remanded the case for further explanation. On remand, Commerce developed a multi-factor analysis and ultimately reversed its position, finding that Nur’s steel scrap was a common, unprocessed input used in various products and industries, and that Nur’s primary business activity—shipbuilding—was not dedicated almost exclusively to producing rebar. As a result, Commerce concluded that Nur was not a cross-owned input supplier, and Kaptan’s CVD rate was reduced to a de minimis level. The CIT sustained Commerce’s remand decision.On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit reviewed the CIT’s decision for abuse of discretion and Commerce’s remand findings for substantial evidence.

Because Commerce's final remand decision is in accordance with law, adequately explained, and supported by substantial evidence, we affirm.

Background

I

The Tariff Act of 1930 permits Commerce to impose countervailing duties (“CVDs”) on merchandise imported from countries whose governments subsidized the manufacture, production, or export of said merchandise. 19 U.S.C. § 1671(a)(1). Commerce subsequently issued a regulation providing that:

Rebar Trade Action Coalition and other domestic steel
producers (collectively, “RTAC”) appeal the decision of the
Court of International Trade (“CIT”), sustaining the final
decision by the U.S. Department of Commerce (“Com-
merce”), which determined that the Turkish government’s
subsidies to Nur, a shipbuilder and co-owned affiliate of
Kaptan, should not be cross-attributed to Kaptan Demir
Celik Endustrisi ve Ticaret A.S. (“Kaptan”).  See Kaptan
Demir Celik Endustrisi ve Ticaret A.S. v. United States, 666
F. Supp. 3d 1334 (Ct. Int’l Trade 2023) (“Kaptan II”).

Because Commerce’s final remand decision is in ac-
cordance with law, adequately explained, and supported by
substantial evidence, we affirm.

Kaptan appealed.  The CIT concluded that Commerce
did not adequately address whether steel scrap was merely
a link in the chain of rebar production or distinguish prior
cases that held that steel scrap was merely a byproduct.
Kaptan Demir Celik Endustrisi ve Ticaret A.S. v. United
States, 633 F. Supp. 3d 1276, 1284–85 & n.3 (Ct. Int’l Trade
2023) (“Kaptan I”).  Accordingly, the CIT remanded the
matter for Commerce to explain its reasoning.  Id. at 1285.

RTAC appeals.  We have jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C.
§ 1295(a)(5).

We have considered RTAC’s other arguments but find
them unpersuasive.  For these reasons, we affirm.

“We are not persuaded,” the Federal Circuit ruled. “Like the Trade Court, we find it noteworthy that at no point during the investigation did Kaptan clarify its supposedly incomplete or inaccurate questionnaire responses, rendering it entirely reasonable for Commerce to rely on the responses Kaptan actually provided.”  
“Kaptan’s questionnaire responses are, self-evidently, strong evidence that the material terms of its sales were not established at the contract date,” the court continued.  
The exporter provided two versions of the contracts, and the first contract said that a size breakdown “would be provided on a date after the date that contract was executed," and the court ruled that “there was no way to be sure that the first contract was merely a draft.”

## News & Updates

KAPTAN DEMIR CELIK ENDUSTRISI VE TICARET A.S. v. US

Authored by: Jeremy J. Gustrowsky

The Federal Circuit affirmed a decision of the U.S. Court of International Trade upholding the Commerce Department’s use of a Turkish steelmaker’s invoice date, rather than its contract date, when calculating antidumping duties. The outcome left Kaptan Demir Celik Endustrisi ve Ticaret A.S. with a final duty rate of 25.86 percent on its exports of steel concrete reinforcing bar (commonly called rebar) to the United States.

Some background helps explain why the date matters so much. Under the Tariff Act of 1930, Commerce may impose antidumping duties when foreign goods are sold in the United States for less than their “normal value,” meaning roughly the price of the same goods in the home market at a time that reasonably corresponds to the time of the U.S. sale. To pin down that moment, Commerce adopted a regulation, 19 C.F.R. § 351.401(i), which says the agency will “normally” use the invoice date recorded in the seller’s ordinary business records, but may use a different date if that other date better reflects when the exporter or producer established the material terms of the sale. Commerce explained when it adopted the rule that price and quantity are often still being negotiated right up until the invoice issues.

Commerce imposed antidumping duties on Turkish rebar in 2017 and later conducted an administrative review covering July 1, 2021 through June 30, 2022. During that period, Turkey experienced hyperinflation, with annualized inflation topping 25 percent for several months. Under the Tariff Act of 1930, 19 U.S.C. § 1202 et seq., Commerce may impose antidumping duties when it determines that a class or kind of foreign merchandise is, or is likely to be, sold in the United States at less than “normal value,” and that such a sale materially injures or threatens material injury to domestic industry. *See* 19 U.S.C.

§§ 1673, 1677b. “Normal value” is the price of the goods in the home market (from which they are exported) at a “time reasonably corresponding to the time of sale used to determine the export price.” 19 U.S.C. § 1677b(a)(1)(A) . Determining the “time of sale,” therefore, is a necessary step in assessing antidumping duties. A Commerce regulation, 19 C.F.R. § 351.401(i) , implements this statutory provision by treating the “time of sale” as the “date of sale” and describing how to determine the date of sale. Specifically, § 351.401(i) directs: In identifying the date of sale of the subject merchandise or foreign like product, the Secretary normally will use the date of invoice, as recorded in the exporter or producer’s records kept in the ordinary course of business. However, the Secretary may use a date other than the date of invoice if the Secretary is satisfied that a different date better reflects the date on which the exporter or producer establishes the material terms of sale. (“Kaptan”) appeals a judgment of the U.S. Court of Inter-national Trade (“Trade Court”) upholding the Department of Commerce’s (“Commerce”) use of Kaptan’s invoice date as the “date of sale” for purposes of calculating an anti-dumping duty rate.  We affirm. ... Consistent with § 351.401(i), Commerce used Kaptan’s invoice date as the date of sale.  Doing so, Commerce found that Kaptan had made sales of rebar to the U.S. at prices below normal value and, consequently, assigned Kaptan a preliminary dump-ing margin of 29.30%.   ... The Trade Court sustained Commerce’s dumping rate.  It determined that substantial evidence supported Com-merce’s use of the invoice date as Kaptan’s date of sale and further supported the agency’s rejection of Kaptan’s re-quest that it use the contract date instead.  The Trade Court decided it need not resolve whether Commerce had authority to adopt § 351.401(i), given that there was no dis-pute between the parties about the “ambiguity or meaning of the statute” the regulation was implementing.  J.A. 9 n.4.   ... In particular, according to Kaptan itself, during the POR the parties to Kaptan’s U.S. sales could amend the shipment date, size breakdown,3 and quantity of goods in-volved in a transaction until the date the goods were shipped or invoiced.  J.A. 467 (“For U.S. sales, the parties may amend the latest shipment date, size breakdown, and, to a lesser extent, quantity until the goods are shipped/in-voiced.”). ... On appeal, Kaptan insists that Commerce erred by re-lying on its questionnaire responses, due to purported in-accuracies in them.  We are not persuaded.  Like the Trade Court, we find it noteworthy that at no point during the investigation did Kaptan clarify its supposedly incomplete or inaccurate questionnaire responses, rendering it en-tirely reasonable for Commerce to rely on the responses Kaptan actually provided. On August 31, 2023, Kaptan filed a case brief with Commerce, arguing that the agency should have used the contract date as the date of sale, and should not have used the invoice date for this purpose. Emphasizing that hyperinflation occurred during the POR, Kaptan asserted that prices in Turkey had rapidly increased between the contract date – when Kaptan had purportedly negotiated the material terms of sale with its U.S. counterparts – and the later invoice date, when Kaptan delivered specific quantities of rebar to the U.S. The Trade Court sustained Commerce’s dumping rate. US 7 III Kaptan makes two principal arguments on appeal. First, it argues that Commerce exceeded its statutory authority under the Tariff Act by adopting a regulatory presumption that the date of sale is the invoice date. Second, it contends that Commerce’s use of the invoice date in this case is not supported by substantial evidence. A Kaptan’s efforts to manufacture an issue of statutory interpretation fail. As the Trade Court correctly noted, the parties do not actually have any disagreement over the meaning of any statutory term. To the contrary, both Kaptan and Commerce agree that “time of sale” means the date on which the material terms of the transaction are established, just as Commerce has defined it in 19 C.F.R. § 351.401 (i). Commerce found that the appropriate date of sale was Kaptan’s invoice date. Kaptan argues that Commerce should have, instead, used the contract date. Like the Trade Court, we conclude that substantial evidence supports Commerce’s decision to use the invoice date.  ... US , No. 25-1559 (Fed. Turkish steel producers, including Kaptan Demir Celik Endustrisi ve Ticaret A.S., were subject to a countervailing duty (CVD) order after the U.S. Department of Commerce determined that the Turkish government subsidized steel rebar exports. During an administrative review, Commerce found that Kaptan sourced steel scrap, a key input for rebar, from several affiliates, including Nur, a shipbuilder.
As a result, Commerce concluded that Nur was not a cross-owned input supplier, and Kaptan’s CVD rate was reduced to a de minimis level. The CIT sustained Commerce’s remand decision. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit reviewed the CIT’s decision for abuse of discretion and Commerce’s remand findings for substantial evidence.
The Federal Circuit affirmed, holding that Commerce’s determination that Nur’s steel scrap was not primarily dedicated to Kaptan’s rebar production was adequately explained, supported by substantial evidence, and consistent with the applicable regulation.
